passage: In the college canteen, Irfan's phone buzzed for the fifth time that hour. Vidya: "Are you upset with me? You replied short." He typed "No, just in class" and felt his shoulders sag. He cared about her. But since the exam results the questions came all day: was the dress okay, was he still coming, was her message rude. That evening they sat on the library steps. "I'll always answer the big ones," Irfan said. "But when you're spinning on small ones, could you try your breathing exercise first, or write it down, and then text me if it's still there?" Vidya's eyes filled. "I thought you were tired of me." "Not of you. Of being your only calm." She nodded slowly. The next day there were three texts, not twelve.

qa.q: What did Vidya's fifth text ask?
qa.a: "Are you upset with me? You replied short."

qa.q: What do Irfan's sagging shoulders suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is tired and drained by the constant reassurance, even though he cares about her.

qa.q: What request did Irfan make on the library steps, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He promised to answer the big worries but asked Vidya to try her own calming steps first on small ones, caring for her without carrying it all.

qa.q: How did Vidya first take Irfan's request?
qa.a: Her eyes filled and she thought he was tired of her, until he explained it was about being her only calm.

grounding: A young man drained by his girlfriend's constant requests for reassurance keeps caring while encouraging her own calming steps.

passage:
Usha,
I'm writing this because when we talk about it, you apologise so fast that I never finish a sentence. I love that you tell me what scares you. I want to keep hearing it. But lately I've been answering the same questions ten times a day: did I lock the door, is the landlord angry, did your mother sound cold on the phone. By night I'm so drained I have nothing left to give, even for the big worries. So here's an idea, not a rule. Before you ask me, could you try the walk round the block, or the worry notebook you liked last year? If it's still there after, ask me, and I'll answer properly. I'm not going anywhere.
Mridul

qa.q: Which notebook does Mridul mention?
qa.a: The worry notebook Usha liked last year.

qa.q: How does Mridul feel by night after answering the same questions all day?
qa.a: Mridul feels so drained there is nothing left to give, even for the big worries.

qa.q: What idea does Mridul offer, and why frame it as "not a rule"?
qa.a: Usha could try a walk or the notebook first and then ask; calling it an idea keeps the request caring rather than cold.

qa.q: How might Usha feel reading "I'm not going anywhere"?
qa.a: Usha may feel reassured that the request isn't rejection, which makes the new routine easier to try.

grounding: A partner worn down by repeated reassurance writes with love, asking the other to try their own calming routines first.

passage: In their house at the edge of the village near Moga, Gurpreet asked Rashmi the same questions every night. 'Did I lock the gate? Is Bebe angry with me? Did the buffalo look sick to you?' Rashmi answered each one. The gate was locked; Bebe was not angry; the buffalo was fine. Then he asked again. By the third month she was lying awake, tired to her bones, feeling she had married his worries too. One night she sat up and took his hand. 'I love you. I will always tell you the truth. But I can't be the lock on every worry. Let's check the gate together once, and then you write the rest in this notebook, and in the morning we'll see which ones came true.' Gurpreet looked hurt, then relieved. In the morning they read the list together. None had.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet ask about the buffalo?
qa.a: Whether it looked sick.

qa.q: How was Rashmi feeling by the third month?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and drained, lying awake, as if she had married his worries too.

qa.q: What did Rashmi offer instead of endless answers?
qa.a: One gate check together, then writing the rest in a notebook to read in the morning, so Gurpreet builds his own way of calming down.

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet look hurt, then relieved?
qa.a: He may have felt rejected at first, then relieved to have a plan and to hear that she loves him and will always tell the truth.

grounding: Shows a young wife drained by her husband's constant requests for reassurance, who offers care while helping him build his own calming routine.

passage: In their small flat in Gothenburg, Astrid had a question for every quiet moment. 'Do you think Elin was annoyed when I left early? Should I text her? Are you sure you're not bored of me?' Freya answered, again and again, until one Sunday she noticed she was dreading the sound of Astrid's voice in the hallway. That frightened her more than anything. That evening she made cocoa and sat beside Astrid on the sofa. 'I'll always answer you honestly. But when I'm the only thing that calms you, I get worn out, and I don't think it really helps you either.' Astrid's eyes filled. 'So what do I do?' 'Maybe the running club you keep talking about. And the list the counsellor gave you. I'll still be here after.' On Tuesday Astrid came back from her first run pink-cheeked, and didn't ask a single worried question all evening.

qa.q: What did Astrid ask about Elin?
qa.a: Whether Elin was annoyed when Astrid left early.

qa.q: What did Freya feel when she noticed she was dreading Astrid's voice?
qa.a: Freya felt frightened and worn out, realising the constant reassuring had drained her.

qa.q: Why was Freya's suggestion kind as well as firm?
qa.a: She promised honesty and to stay, while pointing Astrid to her own calming tools, the running club and the counsellor's list.

qa.q: How might Astrid feel coming back from the first run?
qa.a: Astrid seemed lighter and calmer, pink-cheeked, able to settle without asking for reassurance.

grounding: Shows a partner drained by repeated requests for reassurance who offers care but encourages the other to build her own calming routines.

passage:
In the university library cafe, Anand pushed his cold coffee aside. "You went quiet at lunch. Are you upset with me?"
"No," Arnab said. It was the fourth time today. Yesterday it had been a text Arnab left on read; the day before, a joke he didn't laugh at.
Arnab rubbed his eyes. He loved Anand, and he was so tired his exam notes blurred.
"I'm not upset. I'm drained, and that's different." He took Anand's hand. "I want to help. But I can't be the only thing that settles you. What helped before you knew me?"
Anand thought. "Walking. Writing things down."
"Could you try that first, next time the worry starts? Then tell me what you found."
Anand nodded slowly, looking hurt and relieved at the same time.

qa.q: How many times had Anand asked that day?
qa.a: It was the fourth time that day.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when Anand asked again?
qa.a: Arnab felt drained and tired, so tired his notes blurred, while still loving Anand and wanting to help.

qa.q: What did Arnab suggest, and why is it a wise step?
qa.a: He asked Anand to try walking or writing things down first when worry starts, then share what he found; that keeps the care but stops Arnab carrying all of the worry.

qa.q: What might Anand feel when he hears Arnab is drained?
qa.a: Anand looked hurt and relieved together: hurt to hear it, but perhaps relieved to know Arnab is not upset and still wants to help.

grounding: Shows a partner worn out by repeated requests for reassurance who stays caring while encouraging the other to build his own ways to calm down.
